#9628. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9627. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

The training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

We use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

If you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

The commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗

#9626. Docker Compose: the attribute version is obsolete, in CI

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

Docker compose the attribute version is obsolete is a deprecation warning and not an error: on the run we recorded, Compose printed it and still exited 0. The step went red because of the gate wrapped around the command, so there are two things to settle here, one line in the compose file and one decision about what your pipeline counts as a failure.

The recorded run: the warning on stderr, Compose exit code 0 on the next line, and the step failing underneath it because the script read stderr as failure.

Compose ignores the key and reports it. The failure is added by the step around it, which is why deleting the key fixes today and not the next deprecation.

A Compose step turns red while Compose itself is content. The line names your file and then says the attribute version is obsolete, it will be ignored, please remove it to avoid potential confusion. The shape around that text depends on where it runs: our recorded run on a runner printed it as a log line beginning with a timestamp and a warning level, and a developer machine with a terminal attached prints the same sentence behind a WARN prefix, which is the form bassmaster187/TeslaLogger#1347 quotes. In the recorded run the command exited 0 with the warning on stderr, and the step failed only because the script treated any stderr output as a failure.

``Actions log, docker compose config, Compose v5.5.0 time="2026-09-20T10:55:49Z" level=warning msg="/home/runner/compose-version-demo/compose.yml: the attributeversion` is obsolete, it will be ignored, please remove it to avoid potential confusion" --- compose exit code: 0 ::error::docker compose wrote to stderr

Commands write progress, deprecations and hints to stderr, and treating that as failure makes every future deprecation a build break. Let the command decide, and keep the output in the log where a human can read it.

Search the whole organization, not just the failing repository. A generator that emits the key will reintroduce it in the next service, and the second time around nobody remembers why the gate was removed.

Some teams genuinely want stderr to be quiet, for example when a step is expected to print nothing at all. Filter the lines you have already triaged rather than failing on everything, and keep the filter small enough that a new message still gets your attention.

The Compose specification still accepts a top-level version key. The reference we read on 2026-09-20 says the property is defined for backward compatibility, that it is only informative, and that you will receive a warning message that it is obsolete if used. The same page says Compose always uses the most recent schema to validate the file regardless of the version field, which is the part worth keeping: the key selects nothing.

So deleting it changes nothing about your services. What it changes is the stderr output of every Compose command in the job, and stderr is what your pipeline was reacting to.

The first two rows are from our own run on a latchkey-small runner on 2026-09-20, Compose v5.5.0. The wording is quoted from the Compose version and name reference, read the same day.

Deleting the key fixes today. The gate stays, and the next deprecation Docker adds lands in exactly the same place, which is why it is worth spending two minutes finding out which shape you have. In our experience it is one of three: a step that captures stderr and fails when it is not empty, a command piped into a grep under set -o pipefail, or an internal wrapper script that every repository inherited and nobody owns.

The tell is in the log. If the Compose command printed its normal output and the failure line came from your own script, the gate is yours. If the failure line comes from an action you did not write, look at that action before you look at the compose file.

The fix in the file is one line, and the file below is the whole of what Compose needs: services, and the services you want. Nothing replaces the version key, because nothing was using it.

If a tool in your pipeline parses the compose file itself and expects a version, that tool is what pins you to a v1-era schema, not the file. Pin the fix there rather than keeping a key whose only remaining effect is a warning on every command in the job.

Nothing, and nothing is the right answer. On the recorded run the wrapper posted the failure to the self-heal sidecar and the sidecar answered, no repair followed, and the job ended on the exit code our own gate produced. Latchkey carries no pattern for this, and it should not: the command succeeded, and no change to the environment makes a pipeline stop treating warnings as failures.

No. The Compose reference we read on 2026-09-20 says the top-level version property exists for backward compatibility, is only informative, and produces the obsolete warning when used. It also says Compose validates against the most recent schema regardless of the value, so the key cannot pin a schema and nothing replaces it when you delete it.

Not on its own. On our recorded run the command printed the warning on stderr and exited 0, and the services in the file were parsed normally. It breaks a job only where something in the pipeline treats stderr output, rather than an exit code, as the definition of failure.

Because a step around the command is reading stderr. The usual shapes are a script that captures stderr and fails when it is not empty, a pipeline under set -o pipefail whose grep decides the result, or a shared wrapper script inherited from a CI template. The log tells you which: if the failure line is your own text, the gate is yours.

Delete the top-level version line from every compose file, then run docker compose config once and confirm stderr is empty. Search the whole repository, including files named for an environment such as a staging or test override, because Compose reads each file you pass and warns for each one that still carries the key.

#9625. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9624. Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

Microsoft did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in Microsoft Outlook — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including Adobe, Apple, Google and Mozilla.

Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.

Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

#9623. I gave the non-code half of my one-person company to an AI assistant

I'm a solo founder. I build and run Wolha, an AI character chat app, with no team and no co-founder. For a year the hard part wasn't the code. It was the layer around it: media outreach, creator emails, contest applications, five publishing accounts that go cold the moment I stop posting.

Two months ago I started handing that layer to an AI assistant (Pickle). Not "brainstorm for me" — actually doing the work: open the browser, fill the form, send the email, come back with the link.

Code, product decisions, pricing, and anything sent in my own voice to someone who knows me. The line I use: it can do tasks, it can't be me.

The bottleneck moved. It used to be hours in a day. Now it's the number of decisions I can make in a day — the assistant comes back with twelve of them at once, and half are things I should have decided last week.

That last number is the one I care about. An assistant that sends things I wouldn't have sent is worse than no assistant, so most of the setup time went into the permission boundary, not the prompts.

#9622. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

#9621. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

If you've recently tested your website using Google PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse, you may have noticed a new check under the Agentic Browsing category called “ARD manifest is valid.”

Here's a quick way to satisfy this validation using a minimal JSON file, without installing plugins or configuring complex agentic services.

Step 1: Log in to your website's hosting control panel (cPanel, DirectAdmin, or similar).

Step 2: Open File Manager and navigate to your website's document root, typically:

Step 4: Inside the .well-known folder, create a file named:

Your final file path should look like this:

Step 5: Open the file and paste the following JSON:

Step 6: Open the following URL in your browser:

https://yourdomain.com/.well-known/ard.json

Replace yourdomain.com with your actual domain.

You should see the JSON content without a 404, 403, or other error.

Step 7: Run your website through PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse again and check the ARD manifest validation result.

The empty entries array is allowed by the current ARD manifest schema and can pass Lighthouse's validation.

For these cases, you should create a proper ARD manifest with resource identifiers, names, media types, endpoints, and relevant discovery information.

An empty manifest does not advertise any resources. It only provides a valid manifest structure.

Even with correct JSON, validation may fail or the audit may not recognize your file if:

If your website uses a custom document root or a different hosting architecture, place the file wherever it becomes publicly accessible at /.well-known/ard.json.

ARD stands for Agentic Resource Discovery.

Google announced the ARD specification on June 17, 2026, to help AI agents and registries discover and verify capabilities published across the web.

ARD can describe resources such as MCP servers, A2A agents, agent skills, and other tools or services.

An ARD manifest is normally published at:

The ARD v0.91 specification, dated August 26, 2026, requires a top-level entries array but does not require that array to contain any entries.

This explains why an empty entries array can pass schema validation: it is a valid array containing zero resource declarations.

Passing the ARD manifest audit does not mean:

Also, if no ARD manifest is published or advertised, Lighthouse may simply mark the audit as Not Applicable, which is not necessarily an error.

This method is useful for basic manifest validation, not as a substitute for actual agentic resource discovery.

Sometimes, a two-line JSON file is enough to satisfy a technical validation check. Just understand what you're validating! 🚀

#9618. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!

#9617. OpenCode 2.3 Defaults Background Subagents — Parent Sessions Stay Live While Children Report Idle

On 13 November 2026 OpenCode shipped v2.3.0. The release notes are short on marketing and long on the one change that actually moves the needle for anyone building multi-agent loops: subagents now return immediately, continue in the background, and report back whenever they become idle. The parent session receives a session ID at once and can keep issuing work or waiting on other results. When a child finishes (or goes idle while its own nested work is still running) it notifies the parent. The system explicitly avoids treating a partial idle as completion if background tasks remain.

That is the opposite of the blocking model most agent frameworks still ship by default. In the old shape you spawn a subagent, the parent blocks until the child returns a final answer, then you continue. With any non-trivial tool use or nested delegation the wall-clock time compounds and the parent session becomes a single point of serialization. Background-by-default flips the control flow: the parent remains a live coordinator.

The TUI also defaults to lower verbosity: each run of tool calls and thoughts collapses into one activity row. Set verbosity to medium or high if you need the full trace. The desktop app adds a jump-to-message command (Cmd+Alt+G / Ctrl+Alt+G) so you can search earlier prompts in the current session.

These are not speculative features. They are the defaults that change how you structure a session that launches multiple children.

Most production agent loops look roughly like this:

When step 3 blocks, the loop cannot overlap independent work. Background subagents let the parent issue several in parallel and continue reasoning or issuing more work while the children run. The idle-report protocol is the important part: it gives the parent a clear signal without forcing it to poll, and the “still running” case prevents the classic race where a parent acts on an incomplete result.

For CI or scripted runs the same change surfaces a gotcha. If a subagent starts a long-lived process (dev server, file watcher, or any tool that never naturally exits), the parent can hang waiting for an idle that never arrives. The release notes and follow-up commentary call this out. The practical fix is to treat those children as fire-and-forget or to give them an explicit timeout / completion criterion that the harness can observe.

OpenCode’s model is closer to a harness that owns the session lifetime than to a pure library you call from your own process. The parent session stays in the foreground; children are background sessions that share the same process and tool infrastructure. That gives you free concurrency without spinning extra OS processes for every agent, but it also means a hung or misbehaving child can still affect the shared environment (file locks, ports, GPU memory, etc.).

Compare that with a pure MCP-style or CDP-style isolation model (the kind Cloudflare’s Kitesurf or a dedicated browser-agent binary uses). Isolation is cleaner for untrusted or long-running work; the shared-session model is cheaper and faster for trusted local tooling. OpenCode chose the latter as the default and left the more isolated options as experimental flags or future work.

On Windows the process-daemon change for local shell commands is relevant if you are driving the agent from a long-lived desktop process. The daemon survives the parent session better and keeps output across handoffs. That matters when your outer loop is a Windows service, a tray app, or anything that restarts the OpenCode process without wanting to lose in-flight shell state.

Latency-wise the win is obvious for any workload that has independent sub-tasks. The cost is bookkeeping: you now have to handle the idle and “still running” events correctly, and you must decide what “done” means for each child. In a simple sequential agent the old blocking model was easier to reason about. In anything that looks like a real multi-agent or multi-tool loop, the background default removes a serialization tax you were previously paying for free.

If your outer system is already dealing with streaming audio, dual-track capture, or tight latency budgets (the usual Windows WASAPI + STT + overlay path), the same principle applies: keep the coordinator responsive. A parent that blocks on a long STT partial or a tool call that waits for network will miss the next speech segment or the next overlay update. Background subagents (or any equivalent async tool dispatch) let the parent stay in the critical path while the slower work happens elsewhere.

The OpenCode change does not magically solve capture latency or model TTFS. It does remove one more place where an agent framework forces you to serialize work that does not need to be serialized. That is the kind of incremental improvement that compounds when you are already fighting the Windows audio engine, DPC spikes, and network RTT.

A parent that launches two independent children now looks roughly like:

No explicit wait, no thread pool you have to manage yourself, and a defined protocol for “not done yet.”

That is the practical difference between a library that forces you to invent your own concurrency and a harness that ships the common case as the default.

OpenCode 2.3 is a small release on paper. For anyone who has watched a parent session sit idle while three subagents run sequentially, it is the change that finally matches the architecture you wanted.

#9616. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.
