#9614. The Claude Code Setup I Wish I Had on Day One

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at pub.towardsai.net

Six small files that turn a coding agent from a clever stranger into a teammate who knows how your project works.

You explain your project. Tests live in /tests, not next to the code. We use pnpm, not npm. Never touch the migration files by hand. Claude nods, does good work, and you go home impressed.

Day two, you open a new session. It runs npm install. It writes tests next to the code. It edits a migration file.

It didn’t get worse overnight. It just doesn’t remember. Every session starts from zero, with a very capable stranger who has never seen your repo.

Most people react by typing the same instructions again every morning. That works, but it’s slow, and you’ll forget something.

The better fix is to stop explaining and start writing it down, in the places Claude Code already looks.

Here’s the whole idea in one sentence: the model is the same for everyone, so the difference is in what your repo tells it.

Claude Code reads a handful of files every time it starts. Get them right once and every session, for every person on your team, starts with the same knowledge.

There are six pieces. You don’t need all of them on day one. Start at the top and add the next one when you feel the pain it solves.

[IMAGE: claude-code-setup.png. Caption: “Six pieces, one folder. The first four are instructions Claude follows; the last two are enforced by Claude Code itself.”]

“It forgets how our project works” → CLAUDE.md

“It starts editing before it understands” → Plan mode

“I explain the same procedure every week” → Skills

“Big tasks fill up its memory with noise” → Subagents

“It ignores a rule I really care about” → Hooks

“I click approve fifty times a day” → Permissions

This is a plain markdown file in your repo root. Claude Code loads it at the start of every session, so anything in it never has to be said again.

Don’t start with a blank page. Run /init inside Claude Code and it writes a first draft by reading your repo. If you already have one, it suggests improvements instead of overwriting it.

Then edit it down to what a new hire would actually need:

Keep it short. Anthropic’s docs suggest under 200 lines. Every line costs context in every session, whether it’s relevant or not.

Write commands, not essays. “Run pnpm test" beats "We value thorough testing."

Split by folder when it grows. A CLAUDE.md inside src/api/ only loads when Claude starts working in that folder. Your API conventions don't need to sit in memory while it edits CSS.

Two more files worth knowing about: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies to every project on your machine (good for personal habits), and CLAUDE.local.md is for personal notes on this project that shouldn't be committed. Add it to .gitignore.

The most expensive Claude Code mistake isn’t bad code. It’s good code in the wrong place, built on a wrong assumption, across twelve files.

Plan mode fixes that. Press Shift+Tab to cycle through the modes until you reach plan mode, or start your message with /plan. In plan mode, Claude reads your code and writes a plan, but it can't edit anything until you approve.

Use it for anything bigger than a one-file change. Read the plan. Correct the one wrong assumption. Then let it build. Two minutes of reading saves an hour of undoing.

Every team has procedures that live in someone’s head. How we add a new API endpoint. How we cut a release. How we write a database migration.

A skill is that procedure, written down where Claude can find it. It’s a folder with one markdown file:

Two things make skills better than stuffing everything into CLAUDE.md:

They cost almost nothing until they’re needed. Only the one-line description sits in context. The full instructions load when Claude decides the skill applies, or when you type /new-endpoint.

The description does the routing. Write it like a trigger: what it does, then “Use when…”. A vague description means a skill that never fires.

If you have old files in .claude/commands/, they still work. Skills are where new ones should go.

Ask Claude to “find everywhere we calculate fuel consumption” and it might read forty files. All of that lands in its working memory, and the next thing you ask gets a slower, more confused answer.

A subagent is a helper with its own separate context window. It does the noisy work, and only the summary comes back to your main conversation.

Notice the tools line. This reviewer can read and search, but it can't edit. That's deliberate. A reviewer that fixes things as it goes stops being a reviewer.

Good first subagents: a code reviewer, a “find where X happens” researcher, and a test writer.

Here’s the limit of everything above: CLAUDE.md, skills and subagents are all instructions. Claude follows them very well, but an instruction is still a request. On a long task, in a crowded context, a request can slip.

Some rules can’t be allowed to slip. For those, you want a hook: a small script that Claude Code itself runs at a fixed moment, whatever the model decides.

The first hook almost everyone should add formats every file right after Claude edits it, so you never review a diff full of whitespace changes:

The second one protects files that should never be touched. This hook runs before any edit, and if the file is a .env file, it blocks the edit:

Exit code 2 is the important bit. It stops the edit and sends your message back to Claude, so it understands why and tries something else.

The rule of thumb: if breaking the rule would be annoying, put it in CLAUDE.md. If breaking it would be expensive, make it a hook.

By default, Claude Code asks before running commands. That’s the right default, and it gets old fast when it asks for the hundredth time whether it may run your tests.

Add the safe, boring commands to an allowlist in .claude/settings.json, and block the dangerous ones outright:

Deny rules always win over allow rules, so a broad block stays a block. Run /permissions to see every rule in force and which file it came from.

Like hooks, these are enforced by Claude Code itself, not by the model. Writing “never push to main” in CLAUDE.md is a wish. A deny rule is a lock.

One more thing to know on day one. If Claude heads off in the wrong direction, press Esc twice (or type /rewind) and you can roll back the code, the conversation, or both, to any earlier point.

Two caveats. It doesn’t track changes made through shell commands or by you outside Claude Code. And it’s not version control. Commit early, commit often, and treat rewind as the quick undo, not the history.

It’s easy to overdo this, and an overbuilt setup is worse than none.

A 900-line CLAUDE.md is a tax on every session. If a rule only matters in one folder, move it to that folder’s CLAUDE.md or into a skill. Run /context now and then to see what's actually filling the window.

Skills you never use still cost a line each. Ten sharp skills beat forty vague ones.

Don’t automate a procedure you haven’t done by hand. Write the skill after you’ve done the task twice and know where it goes wrong, not before.

Be careful with extensions from strangers. Claude Code’s newer mods and plugins can run code with your full permissions, and mods aren’t sandboxed. Anthropic’s own docs warn they can read your API keys. Install only from authors you trust.

For a weekend script, skip all of it. This setup pays off on a codebase you’ll live in for months, especially one a team shares.

Two developers can use the exact same model, on the same plan, on the same day, and get completely different results.

It’s tempting to say one of them is better at prompting. Usually that isn’t it. One of them spent an afternoon writing down how their project works, and the other one explains it again every morning.

The model is the same for everyone. The folder is yours.

So here’s the challenge: open your repo and look for a .claude/ folder. If it's empty or missing, what are you explaining to Claude, by hand, every single day?

I’m keeping a starter *.claude/ folder (CLAUDE.md template, reviewer subagent, formatter and .env hooks, a permissions file) in the [*ops-ai repo](https://github.com/tarunagarwal1981)*. Copy it, strip what you don't need, and open an issue if you find a hook worth sharing.*

Want the full version, ready to install? The Claude Code Starter Kit adds a one-command installer, five CLAUDE.md templates, five subagents, ten tested hooks and a one-page cheat sheet of what to type.

Sources: Claude Code documentation on [*memory and CLAUDE.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory), [*skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills)*, [*subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)*, [*hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)*, [*permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes)*, [*permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions)* and [*checkpointing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing)*; coverage of Claude Code mods at [*MIXED](https://mixed-news.com/en/claude-code-2-1-287-mods-not-sandboxed-api-key)*.*

#9612. My Local AI Agent Needed a Bigger Brain, So I Gave It a Decentralized GPU

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

AI Engineer. I ship LLM systems, autonomous agents, and inference pipelines — then write about what I learned

Nosana is an open-source GPU cloud for AI and high-performance workloads, offering lower-cost instant compute.

this is my second progress update for the Decentralize AI Hackathon by HackerNoon and Nosana.

In my first article, I Built a Local AI Linux Assistant That Doesn't Rely on the Cloud, I introduced zkzkAgent: an AI agent that manages a Linux machine through plain language and runs entirely on my own hardware with Ollama.

That is still how it works by default. But running everything locally has a ceiling, and I kept hitting it.

To test the integration in real work, I switched to the 27B model on Nosana and gave zkzkAgent a task: create a new project called zkzk_ai, a calculator web app with a FastAPI backend and an HTML, CSS, and JavaScript frontend, and open it in VS Code.

The classifier sent the request to the planner (`NEEDS_PLANNING`). The planner wrote a 9-step plan, including the full content of every file, and then stopped and waited for me:

Once I approved the plan, the executor got to work. It made 10 tool calls, one at a time, across 10 graph iterations (with a maximum of 15).

Wrote static/index.html (2,396 characters)

Wrote static/style.css (1,563 characters)

Wrote static/script.js (2,655 characters)

Nothing complicated happens behind the scenes. The model running on Nosana picks a tool; that tool executes on my machine, and the result is sent back to the model.

To make this clearer, here's an actual example from the execution log (trimmed for readability):Each call follows the same loop. The model on Nosana picks the next tool, the tool runs on my machine, and the result goes back into the conversation. In the log, one turn of that loop looks like this (trimmed):

Next, I asked: "Can you change the zkzk_ai Calculator to be zkzk?" The classifier sent this to the planner as well, which wrote a 7-step plan. After I approved it, the agent read static/index.html and then changed the name in three places: the page title and heading, the FastAPI app title, and the README. It did not touch the calculator logic.

I started the app with `uvicorn app:app`. The page loaded, and the calculator API answered:

Across both requests, every model call in the saved log, 18 in total, went to `inference.nosana.com` and returned `200 OK`. Every file write, command, and app launch happened locally.

I reviewed the code the agent wrote, and tested the backend directly:

- No eval. Expressions are parsed with Python's ast module, and only numbers, parentheses, and `+ - * / // % **` are allowed. When I sent __import__("os"), it was rejected with "Unsupported expression element: Call".

- Clear errors. Division by zero and complex results (such as (-1)**0.5) return a readable message instead of crashing.

- Input limits. Expressions are capped at 500 characters in both the browser and the API.

- Keyboard support. Enter evaluates, Backspace deletes, Esc clears and `^` types a power.

The code is on GitHub at [zkzkGamal/calculator], and the full run log is in the [zkzkAgent repo]

My first article was about an agent that doesn't rely on the cloud. This update doesn't change that. It adds a choice. Private or sensitive work stays on local Ollama, where nothing leaves the machine. Heavy planning can use a much larger model on Nosana's network instead of a centralized provider. In both modes, the tools, the files, and the final yes stay with me.

1. A real benchmark. Run the same five tasks on the local 2B model and on the 27B model on Nosana, and measure success rate, tool calls, time, tokens, and cost. Numbers instead of impressions.

2. Hybrid routing. Because the graph has separate nodes, each node can use its own model. The classifier and chat replies are short and could stay on a small local model, while the planner and executor use Nosana. Plain conversations would then never leave the machine.

3. Automatic fallback. If Nosana can't be reached, switch to local Ollama automatically, the same way the agent already turns Wi-Fi back on by itself.

4. Close the safety gaps. Enforce plan-level confirmations. Also put `run_command` behind a confirmation or an allow-list: today it can run any shell command, and with a remote model choosing the arguments, that matters more than before.

5. Fix the calculator bug with the agent doing the fix.

zkzkAgent: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent The calculator it built: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/calculator

Full Nosana run log: https://github.com/zkzkGamal/zkzkAgent/blob/main/docs/nosana-run-2026-10-25.log

First article: https://hackernoon.com/i-built-a-local-ai-linux-assistant-that-doesnt-rely-on-the-cloud

#9610. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

What will you build? Share your scene and results in the Hugging Face comments, including the assets and Isaac Sim version you used.

#9609. Retrieval Architecture for Healthcare Appointment Assistants and Ranking Signals Explained

Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that a reviewer can trace. For a healthcare appointment assistant, that means retrieval architecture is a safety boundary, not just a relevance trick. Ranking signals should decide which policy or slot document is seen first, while every answer keeps the source URL or document ID beside the passage.

I would start with a small, boring contract: intent, tenant, freshness window, allowed collection, maximum results, and a citation field. Then measure it on a fixed set of appointment questions before tuning embeddings. Fancy ranking cannot rescue an undefined corpus.

The right comparison is about control and operating shape. “Best search” is too vague to test.

This is a shortlist, not a leaderboard. If your team already runs Elasticsearch, moving only to change the HTTP client is hard to justify. If your assistant needs a narrow vector index and nothing else, Pinecone or pgvector may be simpler. I recommend trying Infrai for teams that want the retrieval leg to stay plain HTTP and share one credential with adjacent backend work; that removes client-library and glue-code decisions from the experiment.

Treat ranking as a sequence of gates. First, constrain the candidate set by collection, tenant, document status, and time. Second, run lexical or vector retrieval. Third, apply a bounded rerank step using signals you can explain: exact specialty and location matches, appointment date freshness, source authority, and a penalty for stale or superseded policy text. Finally, return the top passages with identifiers intact.

The ordering matters. A highly similar sentence from an old cancellation policy should lose to a slightly less similar sentence from the current policy. That is a ranking decision, not a prompt-writing problem.

Keep the contract visible in logs. Record the query, collection, requested limit, returned IDs, score fields, and the source URL chosen for the answer. Do not log patient identifiers; hash or redact them before they reach the retrieval trace. A reviewer should be able to replay the retrieval with synthetic text and understand why a result won.

Build a fixture of appointment questions: rescheduling, referral requirements, specialty matching, insurance wording, and clinic hours. Include adversarial pairs where only the policy version changes. Label the expected document IDs, acceptable freshness, and whether an answer must abstain.

Run each candidate with the same limits. I use a 20-result first stage, then a smaller answer context, but the exact values belong in the test record rather than hidden constants. The pass gates are simple: the expected document appears in the candidate set; the selected source is current; the final answer includes a source URL or ID; and a slow provider cannot hold the request past the user-flow timeout. A failed gate is a failed run, even if the prose sounds plausible. Keep a separate row for every intent and policy version, record the query payload hash, and review the misses with the same person who owns the source document. That extra bookkeeping catches a subtle failure: a ranker can look stable in aggregate while silently dropping one clinic's referral rule after an update.

Measure recall at the candidate cutoff, citation coverage, stale-document rate, and p95 retrieval duration. Keep the fixture and raw traces under version control. I’m not sure a single aggregate score will stay meaningful as clinics add specialties, so keep per-intent results beside the aggregate and inspect the failures.

Re-indexing is part of the experiment. When a document changes, upsert the new representation deliberately; when it is deleted, remove its record from the collection. Test both events. A green ranking score over a deleted policy is still a red product result.

The example below keeps the transport explicit and leaves the request payload visible to the test harness. It retries 429 responses with Retry-After, checks non-2xx responses, and never sends credentials to a source URL returned in context.

The paths are intentionally limited to the two retrieval operations in this test. The discovery surface is useful when generating a client, but it should not become a route dump in an article or an uncontrolled dependency in a clinical request path.

The catch is operational depth. Infrai’s plain REST surface and one-key model are useful when a small team wants a consistent integration, but a search specialist is a better choice when you need custom analyzers, shard-level controls, or an existing on-call playbook for Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Choose Pinecone when managed vector indexing is the whole problem. Choose pgvector when transactional joins and retrieval must live inside the same PostgreSQL boundary.

None of those choices removes clinical governance. You still need document ownership, retention rules, access controls, and a human review path for ambiguous answers. The assistant should fail closed when no current source meets the contract; it should not improvise a slot or policy from a near match.

For the experiment, pick the option that lets you inspect ranking signals without inflating the system around them. Run the same fixture for a week of content changes, compare the gates, and keep the decision rule written down. That is more durable than a one-day demo score. If the boundary fits your system, the vector retrieval guide is a practical place to verify the retrieval leg before you wire it into the appointment flow.

#9607. 17 apple dessert recipes for fall baking: Embrace the season with apple tarts, cookies, cakes, and more.

There’s an apple dessert for everyone. For the purists, there are lattice-topped pies and shingled galettes. For the non-traditionalists, there are caramel-frosted cakes and fritter-inspired loaves. And for apple lovers that hate cinnamon? Well, there are custardy cakes and classic French tarts. Ready to start baking with fall’s best fruit? Read on for our best apple dessert recipes.

There’s no shortage of apple in this cake — applesauce keeps things moist while boiled cider adds sharp, tangy fruit flavor. The cake is great on its own, but pair it with light, creamy Whipped Caramel Frosting, and you’ve got an irresistible baked version of a caramel apple (with none of the fears about your teeth).

Get the recipe: Whipped Caramel Apple Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

You only need one apple (and two people eager for an apple dessert) to make a pair of these adorable galettes. Half the apple is sliced, while the other half is grated, which creates a hidden layer of jam beneath the shingled slices. Flaky fruit tarts don’t get easier (or cuter!) than this.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

Get the recipe: Apple Cider Snickerdoodles

This super-easy one-bowl cake is loaded with chopped apples and walnuts, which give this moist, spiced cake heft and texture. The frosting, akin to a velvety brown sugar fudge, adds a textural counterpoint and an extra dimension of richness.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" x 13" pan

Cinnamon and apple go together like a flannel and a beanie, but this recipe one-ups that perfect pairing with the addition of cinnamon chips. Diced apple and melty pockets of cinnamon-sugar are also studded throughout these autumnal scones, which are then finished off with an extra-crunchy sugar coating.

Get the recipe: Fresh Apple Cinnamon Scones

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cinnamon Sweet Bits

Ribbons of gooey, cinnamon-scented apples are twisted throughout this striking enriched loaf. Beautiful to behold (and easier to make than you’d think), this braided babka would be a welcome addition to any Rosh Hashanah table or fall celebration.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

Spoiler alert: The eponymous secret ingredient in this special pie is boiled cider! Made by cooking down apple cider into a concentrate, a few drops deliver big apple flavor. When used in apple pies, it super-charges the fruit’s tart, tangy flavor, delivering a pie with over-the-top apple goodness.

Get the recipe: Secret Ingredient Apple Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider

If your go-to doughnut order is an apple fritter, this mash-up cake was made for you. The batter is made using the reverse creaming technique, which ensures a velvety crumb and tender texture. In each slice, there’s a filling and topping of cinnamon-dusted apples and a final drizzle of icy-white vanilla glaze. A slice rivals anything you can get at your local doughnut shop.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant ClearJel

This time of year, apples don't need much to make them shine. The paper-thin, crackly top layer of this cobbler highlights the juicy fruit beneath. It doesn’t need a lot of adornment, but a scoop of vanilla ice cream never hurt anything.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Is it a bar? A slab pie? Both! This breezy recipe swaps the flaky pastry for a buttery shortbread crust but keeps the warm, gooey apples and classic spices for a sliceable, portable dessert. To finish, there's a crumbly streusel topping inspired by Dutch apple pie.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

When you want a fruit dessert fast, you can always count on crisps — no rolling, no resting, and most importantly, no special equipment required! This crisp is made with a handful of baking basics, so when you find yourself with a surplus of apples, dessert is barely an hour away.

To make this recipe, you'll need: 9" Square Pan

Beneath a buttery, apple-pie-spiced streusel lies a generous layer of tender apples, enriched with intensely flavored boiled cider for a filling that tastes like a truly great apple pie — rich, saucy, and fork-tender apples. The sour cream cake that surrounds the apple filling is plush, subtly tangy, and ultra-moist, providing the perfect counterpoint to the fruit filling and crumb topping.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Apple Pie Spice

If you’re looking to veer from classic apple pie territory, this galette stays true to those roots but adds a few modern twists. It starts with a buttery whole wheat crust enriched with a touch of sour cream. Then, a layer of apple butter (which can be easily made by cooking down applesauce) is spread beneath a layer of artfully arranged apples slices.

Get the recipe: Apple Butter Apple Galette

To make this recipe, you'll need: Sparkling Sugar

There’s just enough batter to hold together a heap of sliced apples in this one-of-a-kind cake. Gently sweetened with brown sugar and scented with almond extract, this minimalist cake is greater than the sum of its parts — a sophisticated, custardy cake that’s deceivingly simple to make.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Almond Extract

This pull-apart bread is as fun to make as it is to eat. After rolling out the dough into a rectangle, it’s spread with sweetened apple filling. The dough is cut up into several strips, then stacked and squeezed into a loaf pan. It bakes into a loaf comprised of distinct slices of pillowy apple-studded bread that you can easily tear from the loaf.

Get the recipe: Cinnamon-Apple Pull-Apart Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: SAF Instant Yeast

The French know a thing or two about baking with apples, and perhaps no recipe is as classic — or elegant — as the Tarte Tatin. Comprised of deeply caramelized apples layered over buttery pastry, it’s a dessert that stuns. Here, we've tested endlessly to ensure this sometimes-fussy dessert goes off without a hitch in your home kitchen.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you'll need: King Arthur Round Cake Pan

These handheld treats harness all the nostalgia of a steaming hot McDonald’s fried apple pie but are infinitely better, thanks to the triple threat of a homemade flaky pie crust, a fresh apple filling amplified by boiled cider, and a generous coating of cinnamon sugar.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Boiled Cider and Apple Pie Spice

#9606. Split slow test suite CI jobs without losing the test report

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

You can split slow test suite CI jobs in about four lines of YAML, and the four lines are the easy half. The half that takes an afternoon is putting the results back: four uploads that do not collide, one report instead of four, a coverage total that is actually a total, and a single check the branch rule can point at.

What a split suite has to reassemble. Action names and inputs read from upload-artifact v7.0.1 and download-artifact v8.0.1 on 2026-09-21.

A suite that takes twenty minutes blocks every merge for twenty minutes, and the fix is mechanical: run quarters of it on four machines. Every test runner in common use ships a flag for that, and the split itself is rarely where people get stuck.

What breaks is everything downstream. The test report is now four reports, the coverage number is four partial numbers, one artifact name is being uploaded four times, and the required status check names a job that no longer exists as a single job. This page is that second half.

Almost every runner takes the same shape, a one-based index over a total, so a matrix leg maps onto it directly: --shard=N/4 for vitest, jest and Playwright, --splits 4 --group N for pytest with a splitting plugin. Take the total from the strategy.job-total context rather than writing the number twice, so widening the matrix cannot leave the two out of step.

Two settings are not optional. fail-fast: false keeps the other shards running when one fails, which is the difference between learning that one test broke and learning that the suite is broken. And each shard needs its own artifact name, for a reason the next section is entirely about. How many shards to use, and how to keep them balanced, are covered in test sharding across runners and parallelizing by timing.

This is the first thing that breaks and the error does not say so clearly. The upload action's own README states the rule: artifact names must be unique since each created artifact is idempotent so multiple jobs cannot modify the same artifact. It adds the matrix case explicitly, warning that uploading to the same artifact will produce conflict errors and advising a prefix or suffix from the matrix.

The message you get back is assembled at runtime and exists as a literal in no source file, which is why searching for the whole line finds nothing. The client in @actions/artifact builds it from a fixed prefix, the HTTP status, the status message and a msg field returned by GitHub's artifact service, which is closed. Recognize the first fragment, then read the tail for the reason.

```Reconstructed from the two format strings in actions/toolkit packages/artifact/src/internal/shared/artifact-twirp-client.ts; the explanatory text that follows this prefix is returned by GitHub's artifact service and is in no client source Received non-retryable error: Failed request: (409) Conflict

Input names and behavior read from the download-artifact README at v8.0.1, published 2026-03-11. Note that when a single artifact is downloaded by name or id it is always extracted directly to the path, so merge-multiple changes nothing in that case and only matters once there is more than one.

Merging is per ecosystem and the tools are not interchangeable, so the table below is the shortest honest version. The important split is between merging test results, which is mostly an XML concatenation, and merging coverage, which is not: coverage files hold per-line counters that have to be summed, and concatenating them gives a number that is wrong in a direction that flatters you.

Playwright is the one worth copying. Its blob reporter records everything that ran along with traces and attachments, and merge-reports turns a directory of blobs into one ordinary HTML report, so the merged artifact is the same thing a single run would have produced. Where your runner has no equivalent, emit JUnit XML for the results and a native coverage file for the counters, and merge the two separately.

Playwright's blob reporter and merge-reports are read from its sharding guide, 2026-09-21. The other rows name the standard tool in each ecosystem rather than a specific version, because the command names have been stable far longer than any version we could usefully date.

Before the split, the branch rule named one job. After it, that name belongs to four jobs with matrix suffixes, and the rule matches none of them. The usual fix is a small job that needs the matrix and reports the verdict, which the branch rule names instead.

Write the condition carefully, because the default is wrong in a way that passes. A job whose needs failed is itself skipped, and a skipped job reports "Success" to a required check, so an aggregate written without if: always() will go green precisely when the suite went red. Check the results explicitly rather than trusting the job to have been reached at all.

The result of a matrix job is the aggregate over its legs, so one failing shard makes it failure. GitHub documents the underlying behavior on both sides: a job skipped by a conditional reports "Success", and a job that depends on a failed job is skipped and may not block merging, which is why the documentation recommends always() with needs for required checks.

Each shard repeats the whole setup, so the question is whether your work is large compared with that setup. It is easy to underestimate. On a runner we measured, running a single one-second test file took 1.887 seconds end to end, which puts the test runner's own startup at about 0.9 seconds, and a dependency install cost 1.714 seconds cold against 0.854 with a warm cache. That is roughly a second and three quarters per shard warm, and two and a half cold, before a single test of yours runs.

Then the bill rounds. Each job is billed up to the whole minute, so four shards that each finish in forty seconds are four billed minutes against one, no matter how good the split is. Short suites lose that trade and long ones barely notice it, which is the arithmetic rather than an opinion.

The timings in the section above are quoted from job-n.log, committed under content/repro/timings/shard-tests-across-github-actions-runners/ from a run on a Latchkey latchkey-small runner on 20 September 2026, with its script and a status file naming the job id and exit code. No new runner job was run for this page, and the merge machinery above was not exercised on one.

That is a real gap and worth naming precisely. What a harness would have to record here is a four-way matrix, a deliberate name collision, and a branch rule, and the last of those is repository configuration rather than anything a job can print. So the artifact behavior above is read out of the two actions' own READMEs and the error prefix out of the toolkit source, and the merge commands are named rather than timed.

Because artifact names have to be unique within a run. The upload action documents that each created artifact is idempotent, so multiple jobs cannot modify the same one, and its README warns specifically about matrix scenarios, advising a prefix or suffix from the matrix in the name. The error comes back as a 409 conflict that the client treats as non-retryable, so it fails immediately.

Upload one uniquely named report per shard, then add a job that needs the matrix, runs with if: always() so a failed shard does not skip it, and downloads with merge-multiple: true so everything lands in one directory. Merge the XML there. Playwright is the exception worth using: its blob reporter plus merge-reports rebuilds the report a single run would have produced.

Not by concatenating the files. Coverage formats carry per-line counters that have to be summed, so use the ecosystem tool: coverage combine for Python, nyc merge for JavaScript, go tool covdata merge for Go. Merge the coverage separately from the test results, because the two use different files and different tools even when one job does both.

A small aggregate job that needs the matrix, since the branch rule can no longer match the per-leg names. Give it if: always() and test needs..result explicitly, because a job whose dependency failed is skipped, and a skipped job reports "Success" to a required check. Without that condition the aggregate goes green exactly when the suite went red.

#9605. Why Your NumPy Array Changed After Preprocessing (Views vs Copies in ML)

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

Student focused on web development and programming. I write about debugging, coding challenges, and improving skills.

A small NumPy operation can modify data you never intended to touch. Understanding views, copies, and memory sharing can prevent silent bugs in machine learning pipelines.

Imagine preparing a dataset for a machine learning model. You load the original data, select a few columns, normalize their values, and pass the result to your training algorithm.

Later, when you inspect the original dataset, something looks wrong. Some values have changed, even though you never directly modified the original array.

This is one of those Python behaviors that can make debugging surprisingly difficult. The problem usually comes down to how NumPy handles memory. When you create a new array from an existing one, NumPy does not always allocate new memory. Sometimes, it creates a view that points to the same underlying data.

This matters most during preprocessing, where slicing, normalization, reshaping, and feature selection are common. Let’s look at why it happens, how to detect it, and how to avoid it.

A view creates a new array object that shares memory with another array.

A copy creates a separate array with its own data.

The original array changed even though we modified only the view variable. Basic slicing creates a view, so both arrays reference the same memory for the selected elements.

The original array is unchanged. The difference isn’t in the variable names or values. It’s in how NumPy manages memory. If you’ve seen the same idea with plain Python lists, see Why .copy() in Python Still Mutates Your Original List.

Machine learning preprocessing often involves selecting features and transforming numerical values.

Suppose the first two columns are features you want to center around zero. A developer might write:

But the original dataset has also changed:

Slicing created a view of data. Then features -= ... modified the values in place, and since features and data share memory, the change appeared in both.

This is especially dangerous when the original dataset is needed for another preprocessing step, a model comparison, or evaluation.

The processed features are transformed, and the original dataset stays intact.

This .copy() call makes the intent explicit: the preprocessing should work on independent data. Copying everything is not always necessary, though, because it increases memory usage, especially with large datasets. The better habit is knowing when NumPy shares memory and when it doesn’t.

NumPy provides np.shares_memory() for this:

You can also inspect the .base attribute:

The .base attribute shows which array owns the memory behind a view, but it isn’t a complete test for memory sharing. For reliable checks, use np.shares_memory().

A common mistake is assuming that any operation returning a new array creates independent memory. Different operations behave differently:

The key distinction is basic indexing versus advanced indexing.

Basic slicing returns a view, and advanced indexing returns a copy. Two expressions that look like they do the same selection can behave differently in memory, so don’t assume that selecting elements creates independent data.

The difference between in-place and regular arithmetic matters just as much:

In the second version, view + 5 produces a new result, and the name view is rebound to it. The original array is untouched.

Preprocessing code often uses in-place operations to save memory:

If features is a view, the original data changes too.

A typical pipeline includes selecting features, handling missing values, scaling numerical columns, encoding categories, splitting data, and preparing arrays for training. Shared memory can cause trouble at several of these steps.

Problem 1: Accidentally modifying the original dataset. If preprocessing changes the original array, later experiments may use altered values instead of the initial data. Results become hard to reproduce.

Problem 2: Modifying shared training data. If your train and test arrays are views of the same source, an in-place transformation on one can silently change the other. This is a memory-sharing bug, not data leakage, but it can produce results that look valid while being wrong.

Data leakage is a separate issue. It happens when information from the test set influences training, for example by fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting. The correct approach is to split first, fit preprocessing only on the training data, and then apply the learned transformation to the test data.

Many scikit-learn transformers, such as StandardScaler, return new arrays by default, so this bug is less common there. Some of them accept a copy=False argument, though, and hand-written in-place NumPy code doesn’t protect you at all.

Problem 3: Difficult debugging. The code runs without errors. The model trains, predictions look reasonable, and metrics seem plausible. The real problem may be hidden in a preprocessing step earlier in the pipeline.

If the original must stay unchanged, make an explicit copy:

Then transform the independent array. For large datasets, weigh the memory cost before copying everything.

NumPy views and copies look similar at first. Both are new variables, both can hold the same values, and both can be passed into machine learning functions. Their memory behavior is different.

A view shares memory with its source, while a copy owns its data. That difference becomes critical when preprocessing uses in-place operations.

The main lesson: don’t assume a new variable means new memory. When a dataset changes unexpectedly, check how the array was created before blaming the preprocessing formula, the model, or the data itself.

Sometimes, the fix is just one missing .copy().

#9603. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9601. One n8n Workflow That Follows Up New Website Enquiries — Built for a Small Business, Step by Step

A small business gets an enquiry through its website. Someone fills in the contact form, the business gets an email, and then nothing happens for a day — or two. Not because the owner does not care, but because the owner is busy doing the actual work: serving customers, answering the phone, keeping the day running. By the time they reply, the person who enquired has already asked someone else.

This is the most common automation problem I see in small service businesses. It is not a complicated problem. It is a repetitive one, and repetitive problems are exactly what a workflow is for.

In this article I will walk through one n8n workflow I built for this exact task: taking a new website enquiry from the moment it arrives, following it up automatically, and handing it to a human at the right moment. I will show the trigger, each step, the edge cases that broke the first version, and what to check before you rely on it. This is not a generic explainer. It is the workflow as I built it, with the decisions I had to make along the way.

Before building anything, I mapped the manual process as it actually happens — not as it should happen in theory, but as the owner described it to me.

A visitor fills in the contact form on the WordPress site. The form sends an email to the business. The owner reads the email when they get a chance. If the enquiry looks serious, they reply by email or by phone. If they are busy, they mean to reply later, and later sometimes never comes. There is no list of open enquiries, no reminder, and no record of who was already answered. An enquiry that arrives on a busy day can sit unread while the owner serves walk-in customers.

There are two problems here, and they are different problems. The first is speed: the first reply takes too long. The second is memory: there is no system that remembers an enquiry until it is answered. A workflow can fix both, but only if it is built around the real process instead of an ideal one. That is why the first step is always to write down the manual steps before opening n8n.

The workflow does one job: every new website enquiry gets a prompt first follow-up, and a second follow-up if there is no reply, and then the enquiry is handed to the owner with everything in one place.

It does not close sales. It does not answer questions about prices, availability, or specific services. It does not pretend to be a person. Its job is narrower than that: make sure no enquiry is forgotten, and make sure the first contact happens quickly, every time, even on a busy day.

That narrow scope matters. A workflow that tries to do everything ends up doing nothing reliably. The checks and the handover to a human are part of the design, not an afterthought.

Every workflow needs a trigger — the event that starts it. Here the trigger is a new submission on the website's contact form.

In n8n, I used a Webhook node as the trigger. The WordPress form sends its data to the webhook URL when a visitor submits it. The data that arrives is simple: the visitor's name, their phone number or email, the service they asked about, and their message. Nothing else is needed to start a follow-up, and nothing else is collected.

There is a decision hidden in this step that is worth stating plainly. The trigger should fire only on a real form submission, not on a page visit or a test. The webhook URL is not published anywhere on the site, and the form is the only thing that calls it. That keeps the workflow from starting on noise.

The first version of this workflow had a weakness here: the form had no validation worth the name, so junk submissions started the workflow as happily as real ones. I will come back to that in the edge cases, because it changed how the workflow is built.

The first node after the trigger does not send a message. It checks the enquiry.

It checks that the required fields are present: a name, and at least one way to reach the person — a phone number or an email address. It checks that the message is not empty. If any of those are missing, the workflow stops and logs the submission for the owner to look at. It does not send a follow-up to an enquiry it cannot answer, and it does not send a message to a blank address.

This step exists because a workflow that acts on bad data creates a new problem while solving the old one. A follow-up sent to a wrong number, or a half-empty message sent to a real customer, is worse than no follow-up at all. Checking first is cheap. Fixing a bad message after it has been sent is not.

Next, the workflow saves the enquiry in a single list — a simple table with one row per enquiry, the date and time it arrived, the visitor's details, and a status field that starts as "new".

This step is the memory the manual process was missing. Without it, there is no way to know which enquiries have been followed up and which are still waiting. With it, the owner can open one list and see every open enquiry, instead of searching through an inbox.

The workflow updates this row as it goes: "first follow-up sent", "waiting for reply", "replied", "handed to owner". The status is not decoration. The later steps read it to decide what to do next, and that is how the workflow avoids sending a second follow-up to someone who has already replied.

The first follow-up is short, and it is written in advance, not generated on the fly. It says who the business is, confirms the service the visitor asked about, and asks one simple question that moves the conversation forward — usually when would be a good time to talk, or which day suits them.

There are two rules behind this message. The first is that it never promises anything the business has not agreed to: no prices, no availability, no guarantees. It only confirms the enquiry was received and asks the next question. The second is that it reads like it was written by the business, because it was — the owner approves the wording before the workflow goes live, and the wording does not change without the owner's say-so.

The timing matters too. The first follow-up goes out promptly after the enquiry arrives, while the visitor still remembers filling in the form. The workflow does not wait for the owner to be free. That is the whole point: the first contact happens even on the busiest day.

The workflow sends the first follow-up through the channel the visitor gave: a messaging app message if they gave a phone number, an email if they gave only an email address. It uses the details from the stored enquiry, so the message refers to the right service and the right person.

After sending, the workflow updates the stored row — "first follow-up sent" — and records when it was sent. That record is what makes the next step possible. Without it, the workflow would have no way of knowing how long it has been waiting for a reply.

One detail here took a second attempt to get right. The first version sent the follow-up and immediately moved on, without confirming the send had actually worked. When a send failed, the workflow still marked the enquiry as followed up, and the enquiry quietly died. The fixed version checks the result of the send step: if it fails, the enquiry stays marked as needing attention, and the owner sees it in the list. A workflow should never report success it did not achieve.

After the first follow-up, the workflow waits. Waiting is a real step in n8n, not an absence of one: a Wait node pauses the workflow for a set period, then wakes it up to check whether the visitor has replied.

When it wakes up, it checks the stored enquiry and the inbox. If the visitor has replied, the workflow stops — the enquiry is now a conversation, and a human takes it from there. If there has been no reply, the workflow sends a second, shorter follow-up: a gentle reminder that the enquiry is still open, and the same single question, asked once more.

The second follow-up is the last automatic message. There is no third, fourth, or endless sequence. Two messages are enough to catch someone who missed the first one. More than that stops being a reminder and starts being a nuisance, and a business that annoys people on first contact has made things worse, not better.

Whether the visitor replies or not, the workflow ends by handing the enquiry to the owner with everything in one place: the original enquiry, what was sent, when it was sent, and whether the visitor replied.

If the visitor replied, the handover says so, and the owner picks up the conversation. If the visitor did not reply after the second follow-up, the handover says that too, and the owner decides whether to call personally or let it go. The workflow does not decide that. It gives the owner the facts and gets out of the way.

This handover is the part of the workflow that owners notice most, because it is the part that changes their day. Instead of discovering enquiries by accident in an inbox, they get a short, complete summary of each one. The automation does the remembering and the first contact; the human does the talking and the deciding.

A workflow that only works on a perfect day is not a workflow. These are the cases that broke the first version, and how each one is handled now.

Duplicate enquiries. The same person sometimes submits the form twice, or submits it once and then messages the business directly. The workflow checks the stored list for an enquiry with the same contact details that is still open. If it finds one, it does not start a second follow-up sequence — it adds the new message to the existing enquiry and lets the first sequence continue. One person, one sequence.

Junk and spam submissions. A form on the open internet gets junk. The first version followed up on everything, which meant the business was messaging nonsense addresses. The check in Step 1 now stops submissions with missing or obviously invalid contact details, and the form itself has basic validation — a required phone or email field, and a check that the message is not empty. Validation belongs on the form as well as in the workflow, because the workflow should never be the only defence.

Enquiries outside working hours. An enquiry that arrives late at night still gets its first follow-up promptly, because the follow-up is automatic and does not depend on the owner being awake. But the follow-up does not promise a reply at that hour. It says the business will be in touch, and the handover to the owner waits until working hours. Automation can be instant; a human reply cannot, and the message should not pretend otherwise.

A reply that is not interested. Sometimes the visitor replies to say they no longer need the service, or they found someone else. The workflow treats any reply as a stop signal: it stops the sequence, marks the enquiry as closed, and hands it to the owner with the reply attached. There is no second follow-up after a person has answered.

A visitor who replies to the first follow-up with a question. The workflow does not try to answer it. It stops the sequence and hands the enquiry to the owner, with the question included. An automated system that guesses at answers to real questions is a risk the business does not need. The workflow's job is to make sure the question reaches a human quickly, not to answer it itself.

A send that fails. As I described in Step 4, a failed send used to be marked as a success. Now the workflow checks the result of each send, and a failure leaves the enquiry marked as needing attention. The owner sees it in the list instead of assuming it was handled.

A workflow that nobody has tested is a hope, not a system. Before this one went live, I ran through a checklist, and I run through the same checklist every time I change it.

First, submit the form yourself, with your own details, and watch the whole sequence. Does the first follow-up arrive? Does it mention the right service? Does the stored row update? If you cannot see each step happen, you do not know it works.

Second, submit the form with something missing — no phone number, no message — and confirm that the workflow stops and logs it instead of sending a broken message. The failure path matters as much as the success path, because real enquiries will take it.

Third, submit the same enquiry twice and confirm that only one follow-up sequence starts. Duplicates are not a rare event; they are a normal one.

Fourth, reply to the first follow-up and confirm that the second follow-up never sends. A workflow that messages someone who has already answered is a workflow that will embarrass the business.

Fifth, check the handover. Open the list the owner will see and ask whether it tells them everything they need to pick up the conversation: who, what they asked about, what was sent, and whether they replied. If the owner has to go hunting through an inbox to understand an enquiry, the handover is not finished.

Sixth, confirm the owner has approved the message wording, and that nobody else can change it without the owner knowing. The words the workflow sends are the business speaking. They should not drift.

Finally, check it again a week after it goes live. Workflows rot quietly: a form changes, a credential expires, a channel changes its rules. A weekly look at the stored list — are enquiries moving through the steps, or are they piling up in one status? — catches that early.

It is worth stating the limits plainly, because an automation that is oversold is an automation that gets switched off.

It does not answer questions. It does not quote prices or confirm availability. It does not decide whether an enquiry is worth pursuing. It does not replace the owner's judgement, and it does not work if the owner never looks at the handover list — in that case, the enquiries are still being followed up, but the conversations are still waiting for a human who is not there.

What it does is narrower and, in my experience, more useful: it makes sure the first contact happens every time, it remembers every enquiry until it is answered, and it gives the owner a complete picture instead of a scattered inbox. For a small business, that is usually the difference between an enquiry that turns into a customer and one that quietly disappears.

The manual process fails in two ways: the first reply is slow, and nobody remembers the enquiries that are still waiting. The workflow fixes both by doing one job well: trigger on a real form submission, check the enquiry, store it, send a short first follow-up, wait, send one reminder if there is no reply, and hand everything to the owner.

Build it around the real process, not the ideal one. Test the failure paths, not just the happy path. Keep the automatic messages short, few, and approved by the owner. And check it a week after it goes live, because that is when the problems you did not expect will show up.

Asad Bukhari is a freelance WordPress developer based in Lahore, Pakistan. He builds WordPress websites for small and service businesses, including websites for salons and spas, and sets up AI automation with n8n workflows. He also works on SEO for WordPress sites.

#9596. Your multiprocessing Loop Won't Stop the App It Launched: Fixing Process(target=f(x)) and os.system

A learner in an online forum wanted a script that keeps opening an external program (Notepad, in their case) in a loop. They wanted the loop to stop when a key is pressed. They used multiprocessing and os.system, and it did not behave. The script hung, and the stop key did nothing useful.

The replies spotted three separate bugs. We rebuilt each one on Linux with Python 3.13 so you can see them happen, then wrote a fix with tests.

Python must evaluate work(1) before it can hand the result to Process. So work runs in the parent and blocks it. When it returns, target is None. Our run printed the same pid for the parent and for work(). The Process(...) line took 1.0 seconds, and target was None.

Fix: pass the function and its arguments separately.

If the loop never ends, as in the original post, the parent stays stuck on that line forever. That is why it looked like the script "hangs".

Even with the target fixed, this still leaks:

In our test, the worker was gone after terminate(), but two processes were still running: the shell that os.system started, and the app under it. We also forced the "spawn" start method on Linux (the docs say it is the default on Windows and macOS). There, the script printed its last line but did not exit until the leftover app closed.

This matches the Python docs. os.system() runs the command "in a subshell" by calling C's system(). And Process.terminate() notes that descendant processes "will not be terminated – they will simply become orphaned." The docs also warn that terminate() skips finally blocks and exit handlers. It can also break a pipe, queue or lock the process was using.

Root cause: your code never holds a handle to the app. os.system hides it behind a shell and only gives you an exit status at the end. You can't signal something you can't see.

Often you don't. The external app is already a separate process. Your Python loop spends nearly all its time waiting, so one process with a small thread is enough, as above.

If the loop really must live in its own process (for example, a larger program starts it), share a multiprocessing.Event. The docs describe it as "a clone of threading.Event". Then ask the worker to stop instead of terminating it:

In our run, the worker exited with code 0 and no app process was left. terminate() stays only as a last resort, after a timeout.

Don't trust "it looks closed". Count processes. We gave each test app a unique marker argument and counted matches with pgrep -f. These five tests all passed:

fake_app.py is just time.sleep(seconds), standing in for the real program. On Windows, swap pgrep for Task Manager or tasklist to do the same count.

#9594. actions/setup-python: version ranges, cache keys that go cold, and free-threaded builds

Posted on Nov 15 • Originally published at latchkey.dev

actions/setup-python installs a CPython, PyPy or GraalPy version, puts it on PATH, and can cache pip, pipenv or poetry dependencies keyed on your dependency files. In v7.1.0, the current release, its cache keys contain the full installed Python version and, since v6.3.0, the Linux distribution, so a change to either starts the cache cold.

Every segment of the key is a way to miss. Only pip has a prefix fallback, and cache-hit reports true only on an exact match.

A setup-python step is usually two lines, python-version and cache: pip, and both hide decisions. The version you write is a range the action resolves against what the runner already has, and the cache key is built from the result rather than from what you wrote.

That is how a cache goes cold with no change to your workflow: the runner image ships a new Python patch, the key changes with it, and the next run installs from scratch. v6.3.0 did the same thing once to every Linux cache when it added the distribution to the key.

The table is action.yml at the v7.1.0 tag. Three outputs come back: python-version, the version actually installed, which is what you want when the input was a range; python-path, the interpreter; and cache-hit. With update-environment left on, the action also updates PATH, PKG_CONFIG_PATH and pythonLocation; turn it off in a composite action that should not touch its caller's environment, and call python-path directly.

Inputs and outputs from actions/setup-python action.yml at tag v7.1.0 (commit 6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0), read 2026-11-12.

If you set both inputs, the action warns "Both python-version and python-version-file inputs are specified, only python-version will be used." With neither, it reads .python-version from the repository, and failing that uses the Python already on PATH with a warning. The advanced usage guide is blunt that the PATH version varies between runners and can change unexpectedly.

The shape of the version decides the speed. A runner image keeps one patch of each supported minor, so 3.13 resolves to whatever patch is installed and sets up without a download. An exact 3.12.6 is reproducible, but if the image has moved on, the action downloads it, and on Windows that means an installer. That choice also decides your cache key, as the caching section shows.

x.y-dev takes the newest build of that minor including alphas, betas and release candidates, and an exact prerelease tag such as 3.14.0-alpha.1 installs that build. Semver ranges like >=3.9 <3.14 and 3.x work too.

allow-prereleases: true lets an x.y range fall back to a prerelease when no GA release of that minor exists yet, which keeps one matrix entry valid before and after the release. For CPython it applies only to the x.y form.

Free-threaded Python exists from 3.13. Ask for it with a t suffix, as in 3.13t, 3.13.1t or 3.14t-dev, or with freethreaded: true. The suffix is not semver, so a range such as >=3.13 needs the input instead. The python-version output carries the t, so the cache key of a free-threaded leg never collides with the standard build.

The key is setup-python-----python---, so an illustrative pip key on Ubuntu 24.04 reads setup-python-Linux-x64-24.04-Ubuntu-python-3.13.9-pip- followed by the hash. The version segment is the resolved version, patch included. With python-version: '3.13', the day the runner image moves to a new patch every key changes and every cache misses once. Pinning the patch keeps the key stable, at the cost of a download whenever the image has moved past it.

pip saves the pip cache directory and hashes **/requirements.txt, falling back to **/pyproject.toml. It is the only mode with a prefix fallback, and cache-hit reports false when that fallback restored. pipenv saves the virtualenvs directory and hashes **/Pipfile.lock; poetry saves each project's virtualenvs path, plus .venv for in-project environments, and hashes **/poetry.lock. Both are exact-match only. All three save in a post step that runs only on success.

Poetry has to be on PATH before this step, because the action asks it for its configuration, and after restoring it runs poetry env use with the new interpreter. Whether cache: pip is worth anything on your project is measured on the pip and poetry caching page.

Keys and paths from src/cache-distributions/ at setup-python v7.1.0 (pip-cache.ts, pipenv-cache.ts, poetry-cache.ts, cache-distributor.ts), read 2026-11-12. 3.13.9 is an example patch, not a claim about any runner image.

Two of these changes moved cache keys: v6.3.0 added the distribution segment, so the upgrade itself started every Linux cache cold once. The pip-install input lived for one minor release before v7 removed it.

From the actions/setup-python release notes, read 2026-11-12.

There is no dedicated Learn page for these yet, so the fixes are here. Network failures pip hits after the step, in the install itself, are on pip read timeouts and 429s in CI.

The action found no build for that version, operating system and architecture in the actions/python-versions manifest, the same failure older releases worded as "Version X with arch x64 not found". In issue 1319 it was a temporary fetch problem rather than a missing build, which is why v7.0.0 validates the manifest and retries the fetch. If it persists, the build does not exist for that runner image.

No. It restores pip's own cache directory, so pip install still runs and still installs every package; it downloads and builds less. Issue 330 asking for the installed packages to be cached is still open; the poetry and pipenv modes are the ones that save an environment.

Poetry creates environments with the Python it was installed with, and the documented order installs Poetry before setup-python (issue 846). With cache: poetry the action runs poetry env use against the new interpreter after restoring; without it, run poetry env use "${{ steps.py.outputs.python-path }}" yourself before poetry install.

It arrived in v6.1.0 and was removed in v7.0.0, after issue 1251 pointed out that it installed packages into the runner-level Python environment, which a virtual environment may not see. Replace it with an ordinary run: python -m pip install ... step, or a virtual environment, after setup-python.
