#9591. Restoring Engineering Craftsmanship Amid AI-Driven Speed Demands

When a developer remarks that the spark of coding has gone out, they are rarely mourning the physical act of typing syntax. They are describing the systemic collapse of productive friction—the cognitive tension that occurs right before a mental model clicks into place. Before generative AI compressed the software lifecycle, writing code was an iterative, high-friction loop of hypothesis, trial, error, and hard-won insight. When an engineer spent three hours tracking down a memory leak or untangling a recursive race condition, the eventual breakthrough triggered a potent neurobiological reward: a surge of dopamine tied directly to earned mastery and deep ownership.

The enterprise pivot toward AI-driven volume fundamentally short-circuits this reward mechanism. By replacing manual trial-and-error experimentation with instant token generation, systems compress the hypothesis-test-error-insight feedback loop into a passive copy-paste action. The causal chain is stark:

This structural transformation alters every layer of engineering practice, most notably code review. Reviewing an AI-heavy pull request feels uniquely draining because it is no longer a collaborative dialogue about another human engineer's mental model and architectural choices. Instead, it requires auditing high-volume machine-generated diffs for hidden assumptions and silent failure modes—an exercise in verifying syntax over understanding intent. When companies incentivize pure output volume and fast delivery cycles over internal code elegance, they inadvertently alienate engineers from both the process and the product of their labor.

This dynamic creates a dangerous edge-case trap for experienced practitioners. After four years in the industry, restarting a language like Golang from scratch—as many disillusioned developers do—serves as an intuitive defense mechanism against skill atrophy. However, it introduces its own optimization challenge: knowing high-level software principles makes basic tutorials feel excruciatingly slow, yet staying inside a legacy codebase trapped by sprint velocity expectations drains agency. Reclaiming the joy of coding requires carving out intentional, low-stakes friction outside corporate metrics, deliberately slowing down the feedback loop to allow curiosity and tactile problem-solving to take root once again.

When an engineer types a prompt and receives a pristine, multi-file solution in 400 milliseconds, the brain's dopaminergic reward pathway is starved of its primary catalyst: productive friction. Mechanically, dopamine is not released merely upon task completion; it is triggered by the anticipation and physical struggle during the iterative cycle of hypothesis, syntax error, debugging frustration, and eventual root-cause discovery. Generative AI enacts AI-Driven Compression, bypassing this neural search state entirely. Instead of engaging working memory to map spatial logic and track edge cases, the engineer becomes a passive auditor of machine-generated text. Over time, this shifts the reward schedule from variable-ratio effort to instantaneous gratification, causing emotional flatlining: the engineer hits corporate output metrics on paper while experiencing a profound neurobiological disconnect from the work.

This cognitive detachment bleeds directly into code review structures, transforming what was once a collaborative architectural dialogue into an exhaustive auditing chore. Reviewing human-written code requires evaluating human intent, trade-offs, and craftsmanship choices. Conversely, auditing high-volume AI diffs forces the brain to hunt for silent failure modes and probabilistic hallucinations buried beneath syntactically correct boilerplate. Because the human reviewer did not physically type or mentally derive the logic, their working memory must reverse-engineer the AI's hidden assumptions without the scaffolding of trial-and-error memory. This demands a disproportionate spike in cognitive load, turning code reviews into a primary engine of developer burnout disguised as ordinary workplace fatigue.

Faced with this alienation, engineers often attempt a language reset—such as starting Golang from scratch after years of senior experience—to reclaim a sense of personal agency. However, this strategy carries a severe edge-case trap: if approached with the same sprint-oriented efficiency mindset, the engineer turns low-stakes play into another performance metric, destroying its restorative value. To evaluate countermeasures rigorously, we must weigh options by their capacity to re-engage intrinsic curiosity without triggering corporate metrics:

Decision Rule: If daily production work is dominated by high-volume AI synthesis and low-friction output (X), then the engineer must establish an isolated offline sandbox where tooling friction is artificially maximized (Y). This solution stops working the moment the engineer applies productivity metrics or velocity deadlines to the sandbox, converting creative play back into alienated labor.

When an engineer with four years of experience looks at an IDE and feels a hollow numbness instead of curiosity, they are not just experiencing garden-variety workplace fatigue. They are suffering from a systemic neurobiological deprivation caused by AI-driven compression of the software development lifecycle. To understand why the "spark" vanishes the moment a company demands pure velocity, we have to look past corporate metrics and examine how the human brain actually processes accomplishment.

Dopamine—the neurotransmitter responsible for anticipation, motivation, and the subjective feeling of flow—does not fire as a passive reward for completing a task. It fires during the anticipation phase of problem-solving, specifically when the brain enters an active neural search state. This state requires a precise mechanical sequence: a hypothesis is formed, syntax is typed, a compiler throws an error, working memory strains against a logic gap, and through iterative trial-and-error, root-cause discovery clicks into place. This friction is not an inefficiency to be engineered away; it is the biological engine of mastery.

When generative tools instantly produce syntactically correct boilerplate, they bypass this entire evolutionary feedback loop. The brain experiences an abrupt shift from variable-ratio effort (where rewards are earned through struggle) to instantaneous gratification. The consequence of this shortcut is emotional flatlining. Because code is shipped without the engineer ever forming a physical mental model through trial and error, authorship is decoupled from understanding. The engineer transitions from a creator building a mental architecture into a passive auditor of machine-generated text.

This dynamic radically deforms daily cognitive load, particularly during code reviews. Reviewing human-written code engages shared reasoning, trade-off evaluation, and intent-checking. By contrast, reviewing high-volume AI diffs forces the reviewer to reverse-engineer hidden assumptions and hunt for silent failure modes within code they never mentally simulated. The brain absorbs an immense load just checking for probabilistic hallucinations, yet receives zero dopamine reinforcement in return. The output metrics look pristine on a corporate dashboard, but the internal cognitive machinery is starving.

Attempts to escape this state often fail because engineers fall into the language reset trap. Picking up a language from scratch—such as restarting Golang after years of professional use—feels tedious if approached with a sprint-oriented mindset. If an engineer brings velocity metrics or performance goals into a side-learning project, they merely recreate the corporate treadmill in miniature, converting play back into alienated labor.

To restore that lost dopamine loop, engineers must intentionally establish structural countermeasures:

When you sit down to write code, push a pull request, and realize you feel nothing—no surge of satisfaction upon fixing a stubborn bug, just a hollow sense of transaction—you are not experiencing ordinary workplace fatigue. You are experiencing emotional flatlining driven by a neurobiological deficit. Dopamine is not released upon task completion; it floods the brain during the anticipation phase of the neural search state. When generative AI instantly provides the solution, it compresses the hypothesis-test-error-insight loop, robbing working memory of the friction required to trigger a genuine reward response.

For engineers four years into their career, this manifests as a profound existential mismatch: you entered the field for the craft of problem-solving, but your daily output has been reduced to high-volume AI diff auditing. Reviewing machine-generated code forces your brain to reverse-engineer hidden assumptions and hunt for silent failure modes in foreign boilerplate, imposing a heavy cognitive tax without any compensatory dopamine payout.

To break this cycle, engineers often attempt a language reset—such as restarting Golang from scratch—hoping novelty will restore their curiosity. However, this frequently backfires into what we call the Language Reset Trap.

Decision Rule for Recovery: If your daily production work is dominated by high-volume AI synthesis and low-friction output (X), you must establish an isolated offline sandbox where tooling friction is artificially maximized (Y). Build core components—such as a mini network stack, a parser, or a low-level data structure—entirely from raw specifications without autocomplete, internet lookups, or LLM assistants.

However, this intervention carries a strict failure condition. The sandbox intervention fails instantly if you apply productivity metrics, sprint velocity, or delivery deadlines to your experimental learning. If you treat learning Golang as a key performance indicator or a race to build a production service, you convert creative play back into alienated labor, destroying the cognitive benefits before they take root.

To reclaim the spark, you must decouple the act of coding from corporate output. Protect your experimental space with zero efficiency targets. Let the compiler reject your syntax five times; that very struggle is the physical mechanism through which your brain reconstructs its mental model and restores the dopamine response of earned mastery.

When an engineer with four years of experience looks at a codebase and feels a hollow numbness rather than the old rush of satisfaction, it is rarely standard workplace fatigue. It is a neurobiological deficit. Across the industry, the relentless compression of the software development lifecycle by generative AI has severed authorship from mental model construction, starving the brain of the friction required to trigger dopamine rewards.

Dopamine does not release upon task completion; it surges exclusively during the anticipation phase of problem-solving—the neural search state. When an engineer writes code manually, the brain engages in an iterative loop: hypothesis formation leads to syntax input, compiler feedback strains working memory, and trial-and-error iteration culminates in root-cause discovery. Generative AI short-circuits this entire physical and cognitive sequence. By instantly generating syntactically pristine boilerplate, tools eliminate variable-effort struggle.

The resulting cognitive shift transforms engineers from active creators into passive auditors. Auditing high-volume AI diffs forces the reviewer to reverse-engineer hidden assumptions and hunt for probabilistic hallucinations within unauthored code. This imposes a heavy cognitive tax on working memory while yielding zero dopamine reward, driving emotional flatlining and disengagement even as corporate throughput metrics soar.

To reclaim agency, engineers often attempt side-learning projects or language resets—such as restarting Golang from scratch. However, the choice of intervention dictates whether the spark returns or burnout deepens. Below is an analytical comparison of restorative strategies:

A frequent error occurs when engineers apply sprint metrics, velocity targets, or efficiency KPIs to their side-learning projects. Attempting to master a language like Golang through a lens of rapid delivery turns play into alienated labor, destroying the cognitive benefits of the reset.

To prevent this, engineers must apply a strict operational rule: If daily production work is dominated by high-volume AI synthesis, establish an isolated offline sandbox where tooling friction is artificially maximized. Build core components—such as a mini network stack or parser—purely from raw specifications without autocomplete, internet lookups, or LLMs.

The failure condition is absolute: The sandbox intervention fails instantly if productivity metrics or delivery deadlines are applied. Decoupling coding from corporate output with zero efficiency targets is the only mechanism that allows compilation errors and manual struggle to physically reconstruct mental models and restore the authentic joy of coding.

#9580. This fall, reach for this unlikely apple ingredient : Apple cider vinegar is a baker’s secret weapon.

As fall baking season settles in, you're probably reaching for apples — and the many flavor-packed ingredients they produce. Applesauce cooks down into tangy apple butter to be cradled in a flaky galette, while a drop of boiled cider can deliver supercharged apple flavor to crumb cake. But the baking ingredient you may be overlooking may be something you associate more with salad dressings and wellness tonics: apple cider vinegar.

This tangy, apple-y vinegar is a secret ingredient in some of our favorite fall recipes, including cookbook author Claire Saffitz’s Cinnamon-and-Sugar Apple Pie. While lemon juice is the standard acid used in most fruit pie fillings, Claire opts for apple cider vinegar here to complement the filling’s flavors. “It helps as a flavor enhancer, and I also like that it’s apple cider in an apple pie. It’s a nice symmetry,” she mentions.

Similarly, apple cider vinegar is used in the cooking liquid alongside sugar and butter to caramelize apples in a Classic Apple Tarte Tatin. The benefit is twofold: Vinegar’s acidity helps cut the sweetness of the caramel, and it prevents the apples from getting too mushy, instead maintaining their fork-tender texture.

Pastry chef and cookbook author Natasha Pickowicz often leans into the jolt vinegar can add, including adding a few drops to her cake soaks for an additional layer of flavor. “Cake soaks should have a balance of tart, sweet, and savory notes — just like vinaigrette for your favorite salad,” she writes in her cookbook More Than Cake. It can add intrigue to layered cakes like this Golden Spice Cake or Pumpkin Layer Cake. In her cookbook, she also calls for a glaze spiked with apple cider vinegar to brush onto an apple tart after baking. It’s the finishing touch “to further emphasize the tart’s resolute apple-ness,” she writes.

Apple cider vinegar doesn’t need to be limited to only apple desserts, either. In our Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, we call for apple cider vinegar as a foil to the brown sugar filling’s cloying sweetness. A spoonful of apple cider vinegar may not announce itself boldly, but it makes a small splash for brighter, more balanced bakes.

For more fall baking inspiration, check out our Fall Flavor Edit.

#9573. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

Find our high-extraction Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour online.

#9569. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9565. Ditch The Mayo: Give Pasta Salad A Calcium & Flavor Boost With One Ingredient

Mayonnaise is the thick and creamy matrix that disperses all the other flavors in your pasta salad, coating the noodles and giving the dish a great texture when cold. But if you want more of that tangy, rich flavor, plus a decent boost of calcium, try blending feta with vinaigrette next time for a tasty result.

Feta is a crumbly, tangy cheese with plenty of fat and salt, making it intensely flavorful but also creamy under the right circumstances. When you blend it with a premade vinaigrette, you create a beautifully bright condiment that pairs quite well with just about any type of pasta, from whole wheat to semolina. Unlike mayo, it combines the smooth decadence of dairy fat with fermented complexity and has a thinner texture that sinks into the nooks and crannies of different noodle shapes. While tasty, the ingredients still pair quite well with other pasta salad secret ingredients, from curry powder to various vegetables, so you won't need to switch up your recipe too much.

Daily recommended calcium intake varies quite a bit based on age and other factors, but it starts at around 1,000 milligrams a day for most adults. Getting this much can be a challenge, but feta has about 270 milligrams per 60-gram serving, or about half a cup. Compared to the practically zero milligrams found in mayonnaise, this is an easy way to convert pasta salad into something not only more flavorful, but also more nutritionally complex.

Pasta salad is a pretty flexible recipe, with no real standard ingredients outside of the carb in its name and a dressing. This means you don't have to choose between flavor and nutrition, and there are plenty of ingredients that can check both boxes quite easily.

The false assumption everyone makes about milk is that it's the be-all and end-all of calcium-rich foods, but there are plenty of vegetables rich in the nutrient. A single cup of cooked spinach can add a whopping 240 milligrams of calcium and tastes fantastic with a feta-vinaigrette dressing. It's also quite an unobtrusive vegetable that has little effect on your dish's flavor profile, adding subtle grassy notes that make the end result more complex. If you want to bulk out the texture instead, a cup of cooked broccoli adds about 60 milligrams of calcium and creates a deliciously chewy texture when left a bit crunchy.

Pasta salads are all about selecting the right pasta shape for your dressing. Since this vinaigrette is a bit runnier than mayo, you'll want to stick with varieties that are short and curly, creating enough surface area for it to cling to. While varieties made with traditional ingredients only have about 18 milligrams of calcium per 100 grams, whole grain pasta has 28 milligrams and a more rustic flavor. This can help balance out the acidity of the dressing, giving the dish a great mix of brightness and earthiness.

#9563. Forget Salmon: This Fast-Cooking Fish Has Fewer Calories

Salmon's rich intensity also means it generally has more calories, which can mean different things based on someone's dietary needs. If you're conscious of this and still want something that cooks up quickly (and deliciously), try flounder, a leaner, lower-calorie option that never lacks flavor.

Exact calorie amounts can vary quite a bit, especially when it comes to wild versus farmed salmon, but even the leanest ones usually sit between 130 and 200 calories per three-ounce serving. Flounder populations, however, have a more uniform lifestyle and consistently clock in at around 100 calories per three-ounce serving. That brown or gray layer of fat may help a salmon migrate and survive cold waters, but flounder are sedentary ambush predators that don't have nearly the same energy requirements. On your plate, this means a fillet of flounder is lean, clean-tasting, and quite mild compared to a richly marbled piece of salmon.

Because flounder is often thinner and far less fatty than salmon, that also means it cooks exponentially quicker. While a skin-on fillet can widen your margin of error, it's still much easier to render your tender fish into a dense, rubbery mess. Your best bet is to treat it like a lean steak and use a hot and fast cooking method, letting a bit of carryover cooking finish the center rather than trying to reach the perfect temperature in a pan or on the grill.

Flounder is delicate, light, and can easily lose its natural flavor if seasoned too heavily. While it's not exactly a beginner-friendly fish, the best ways to cook it are often straightforward and focus on timing and temperature, not technique. Hands-off methods that require little manipulation or rely on a sauce for flavor are usually ideal and keep your meat moist and tender.

If you haven't tried making a meunière yet, it's a classic seafood dish you should try at least once. Made by combining browned butter, lemon, and parsley, it's just flavorful enough to elevate your flounder without overwhelming it. Just about any French butter sauce, from beurre blanc to béchamel, is great with flounder because it adds a bit of richness and is a great vehicle for other tasty seasonings. Plus, they're flavorful enough that you'll only have to pan-sear each side of your fish, reducing the chance that it'll fall apart or overcook.

Flounder grows more delicate the more it's cooked, so preparation methods that rely on you only handling it when raw are also quite ideal. Baking is a precise method, and you only have to move the fish once to transfer it to a plate. On the other hand, flounder is fantastic when deep-fried, and the breading helps it hold its shape. You'll still want to use a large, slotted tool and a delicate hand when fishing it out, but all you need to do is batter and drop it into oil for a great result.

#9557. For More Flavorful Fried Eggs, Add A Teaspoon Of This Spicy Ingredient To The Pan

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Know the right fried egg cooking hacks, and your breakfast can easily take on a gourmet twist. For one such easy enhancement, try a hit of spice — just a teaspoon of harissa will effectively flavor eggs. Hailing from Tunisia, this smoky-savory condiment consists of chilies, garlic, and a wide assortment of spices (often cumin and coriander), all blended into a smooth dark-red consistency. It's a bold but not overwhelming blend of flavors that shines alongside eggs in a pan.

For the greatest ease amidst bleary-eyed mornings, you can buy the spice online in the form of paste in a jar or tube. Don't confuse the condiment with powdered harissa seasoning, a dry blend with a similar flavor profile, but not the right composition for this application — though it might do very well mixed into scrambled eggs.

Instead, you'll want a whole teaspoon of the paste itself. Heat up the pan, and throw it into a hot neutral oil, creating an aromatic red bath of chilis and spices. Follow this up by cracking in a fried egg or two, and sizzle up the lot in the fragrant oil. You'll get eggs with a dark red color and a warm dose of spice, making a dish with a lot of flavor yet not much fuss.

Fried eggs make for a wondrously versatile food, fit as both a dish garnish and a meal in themselves. Upgraded with an ingredient like harissa, such versatile applications continue — only now with a bold hit of spice. You can integrate the seasoned eggs into a wide array of dishes.

Start by taking inspiration from çilbir, a Turkish egg dish consisting of poached eggs, pepper-spiced butter, and yogurt. Consider serving the harissa fried eggs atop a thick and tangy dairy canvas, like Greek-style yogurt or salty labneh. Scooped up with bread or pita, it's a satisfying meal that doesn't require much effort. You can also make a quick and easy shakshuka-style fried egg by creating a base of tomato paste and harissa for your eggs to simmer in.

Once lunch or dinner rolls around, add a little heft to the dish. Harissa-spiced eggs make for a great topping atop extra crunchy chickpeas or a creamy batch of white beans. A pork chop topped with a fried egg is a tried-and-true classic, and the harissa element will lend the construction an extra touch of spice. Not to mention, fried eggs belong atop sauteed greens, too; it's a terrific enhancement to a bowl of kale, for example. Harissa-spiced eggs deliver an aromatic punch, making them a culinary combo worth keeping in mind.

#9554. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

Olive oil is a highly coveted ingredient due to its rich flavor, versatility, and numerous health benefits. While they may hold no accolades or Michelin stars, household cooks carry a wealth of knowledge when it comes to which olive oils are best for daily use.

There are plenty of sensational olive oils found at affordable prices, from the mild and mellow-tasting to robust EVOOs bursting with grassy and fruity notes. #9549. The Traditional Kitchen Knife Bobby Flay Recommends Is On Amazon

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Whether you're an amateur home cook or a seasoned chef, a high-quality chef's knife is one of the three knives you need in your kitchen arsenal. However, with so many options out there, choosing the right one can quickly become overwhelming. You'll want something versatile enough to finely chop vegetables, break down a chicken, and handle just about everything in between. Durability matters, too. A good knife should last for years, if not a lifetime, with the right care. And, of course, it needs to hold its sharp edge. Luckily, Food Network star Bobby Flay has a recommendation that takes some of the guesswork out of the process (per The Kitchn): the Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's Knife, available on Amazon.

Before getting into the knife's many selling points, there's one thing we have to address. At $163.95 (which is the sale price — it's normally around $205), it's certainly not a budget-friendly buy. But there are plenty of reasons why we think it could be worth the investment. At its core, knife steel is a blend of iron and carbon, with manufacturers adding other elements to improve its performance. It's these added elements that set Shun knives apart from the rest.

The Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's knife uses a proprietary blend called VG-MAX, which is specifically formulated to resist corrosion and wear while maintaining a sharp edge. It also has a high carbon content, helping the blade achieve the hardness needed for excellent edge retention. The combination of elements in VG-MAX gives the Shun an advantage over many more affordable knives made with lower-grade steel, which have the tendency to lose their sharpness far more quickly with regular use. In other words, you're paying for a knife that's designed to stay sharp, rather than one that needs constant maintenance to keep it performing.

If the name didn't give it away already, Shun is a Japanese knife brand, and all its knives are handcrafted in Seki City, a region renowned for centuries of sword and knife making. Any kitchen nerd knows that Japanese knives are up there with German ones when it comes to quality, so just by looking at the place of origin, you can expect a considerable degree of craftsmanship to have gone into this blade.

Interestingly, despite its Japanese origins, the Shun Classic 8-inch Western Cook's Knife doesn't adopt the traditional santoku shape, often considered Japan's answer to the Western chef's knife. Both blades are versatile, all-purpose kitchen knives, but they differ in their blade profiles and the way they're typically used. Neither is necessarily better than the other; that distinction largely comes down to personal preference and preferred cutting style.

While the blade might not have a traditional Japanese shape, the handle certainly draws on Japanese craftsmanship. It's made from Pakkawood, an engineered composite created by stacking thin hardwood veneers and infusing them with phenolic resin, which is then bonded together using high heat. The result of this admittedly complicated process is a durable, moisture-resistant material that's less prone to warping and cracking than ordinary wood. This makes it easy to keep clean, although that doesn't mean you should put the knife in the dishwasher or leave it to soak in the sink. Even quality materials can't protect even the most durable blades from the harsh detergents, water, and high temperatures, which will inevitably cause rusting and damage over time. Hand-washing and drying your knife promptly remains the better option.

#9548. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

#9544. Skip Regular Butter And Oil: Roasted Potatoes Are 10x Crispier With This Ingredient

A mistake everyone makes with crispy roasted potatoes is using the wrong cooking fat, which tends to burn under the high heat required for great texture. Regular butter and oil each have their strengths, but neither gets quite the same result as ghee, a type of clarified butter with Indian origins.

High-smoke-point oil is great for roasted potatoes because it lets you use high heat to crisp the exteriors. However, it doesn't add much in the way of flavor, so you're missing out on an opportunity to layer on more depth. On the other hand, butter is great at making a hearty side dish, but the milk solids tend to burn at temperatures above 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Ghee, however, has virtually no milk solids and very little moisture, making it the perfect middle ground. With a smoke point of around 450 degrees Fahrenheit and a rich flavor, it's the perfect way to achieve great texture without sacrificing taste.

The biggest difference between ghee and clarified butter is taste and color. The former comes "pre-toasted," giving it a deep golden hue and an intense nuttiness that essentially kick-starts the roasted flavor of your tubers. Even if you don't use the various tricks to increase surface area, your potatoes will taste like they have more crispy outsides than usual. A small amount helps them develop the perfect color, giving you a showstopping presentation that tastes great, looks amazing, and still lets you use your existing favorite recipe with only one ingredient substitution.

Ghee's flavor is more pronounced than butter's or oil's, but it's still just as versatile. Rather than switching up seasoning, it's best to focus on how to increase the "roasted" factor of your potatoes. Increasing their surface area, ensuring they have as little surface moisture as possible, and using the correct type of pan are easy ways to improve their flavor.

There's an easy British trick for roasted potatoes that makes them exponentially crispier: roughing up the exterior. By parboiling them, then shaking them in a colander, you transform the smooth outside into one covered in tiny little ridges and bumps. These have a far greater surface area, which means your ghee has more room to help brown the exteriors, so you end up with more crispiness than normal. Not only does this improve the flavor, but it also speeds up the roasting time since you aren't cooking a raw vegetable.

Moisture is the enemy of crispiness and can prevent even ghee from creating a great texture. If you parboiled your potatoes, letting them steam-dry for a bit makes them easier to work with and removes excess water. If cooking them raw, it may help to pat the pieces dry first to remove excess surface moisture. Either way, a heavy-bottomed pan, preferably cast iron or stainless steel, holds more heat and can develop far better color and flavor than something that is thin, flimsy, or nonstick.

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

To make this recipe, you'll need: Baker’s Special Dry Milk

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Offset Spatula

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Espresso Powder and Bundt Pan

#9539. 10 Protein-Packed Substitutes For Mayo In Chicken Salad

Chicken salad is like edible Americana, a comfort food that's beloved for its taste, nutrition, and versatility. You can find it in the prepared section of your local supermarket or on the menu of your favorite diner. Trying to cut down on carbohydrates? Have a scoop on a salad. Want a light and easy lunch? Have it as a club or between two pieces of toasted whole-grain bread. More importantly, though, chicken salad is like a ball of clay ready to be shaped by your taste preferences. You can take it in infinite directions: Mediterranean, Southwest, Spanish, French, Indian, Vietnamese. Have some extra sprigs of cilantro or half a bag of red grapes lying hanging around the fridge? Add 'em. Don't know what to do with those leftover pecans or knob of fresh ginger? You can throw those in, too.

But the foundation of any respectable chicken salad is its creamy binder. In that regard, mayonnaise is the undisputed classic, turning your basic diced chicken breast into something moist, savory, and luscious. However, plenty of other ingredients deliver that signature smoothness — just with more protein. From tzatziki to silken tofu to labneh, there are tons of options that deliver both texture and an added pop of flavor. Whether you're minding your macros or just looking for a new spin on a classic dish, this list of protein-packed mayo substitutes is for you.

Yogurt has a long and storied reputation as a health food, so long, in fact, that its beneficial properties are documented in Indian Ayurvedic medicinal writings from more than 7,000 years ago. Today, it's seen as a better-for-you breakfast option, loaded with beneficial probiotics, calcium, and, of course, protein. Yogurt, especially the more thoroughly strained Greek variety, has an excellent calorie-to-protein ratio (about 16 grams of protein per 150 calories when made with whole milk), which is why it has become so popular with bodybuilders and wellness influencers.

However, Greek yogurt still has a place in ordinary kitchens, and it's especially useful for people looking for a healthier alternative to mayonnaise, cream cheese, or any other creamy, high-fat, high-cholesterol product, which is why it makes such a great addition to homemade chicken salad. Even when prepared with mayonnaise, chicken salad is a relatively nutritious lunch option, typically made with low-fat chicken breast, fresh herbs, diced veggies, and maybe some nuts or sliced grapes. Whole milk yogurt, which is creamier than low-fat options, builds on that by adding extra protein, moisture, and the richness synonymous with a good chicken salad. It also adds a little tang that complements the subdued nature of poultry and plays well with other common chicken-salad additions, like mustard, dill, or curry powder.

It feels like every week there's another article or study being published identifying the benefits of gut health. This increased focus on the gut microbiome and the trillions of microorganisms that occupy it has brought all sorts of fermented dairy products, which are packed with probiotics and other useful bacteria, back into the nutritional spotlight. In this department, Greek yogurt is king (at least in the United States), but other styles are slowly making their way to the supermarket dairy aisle. One of them is skyr, also known as Icelandic yogurt.

Technically classified as a cheese because its proteins are coagulated with rennet (a naturally occurring enzyme), skyr is dense, almost custard-like, with a mild sweetness and less assertive bite than Greek yogurt. Nutritionally, the two dairy products have an almost identical profile, although skyr is typically slightly higher in protein per serving due to a more rigorous straining process. But it's that straining — and subsequent thicker texture — that makes skyr such a terrific mayo substitute, delivering the same full creaminess without the more forward lactic tang of typical yogurt. How you use it in your chicken salad is a personal preference. If you like your chicken salad on the more unctuous side, use it as is; if you like it a little looser, thin your skyr with a tablespoon or two of milk, which may also help coat each ingredient more evenly.

On a per-calorie basis, cottage cheese is hard to beat among high-protein foods, with (on average) 12-14 grams of protein per 100-calorie serving. Unlike yogurt, which is fermented with bacteria, cottage cheese is made through acidification. As milk becomes more acidic and the pH level drops, the proteins denature, clump, and coagulate into tiny little curds. Although the process is simple, there's a lot of variability between brands. Some are saltier or creamier or contain larger curds.

But the most influential factor, especially regarding your chicken salad, is the fat content. While low-fat cottage cheese has fewer calories per serving, it lacks the richness needed to rehydrate dry chicken. Beyond extra unctuousness, full-fat cottage cheese adds salinity, clean milky notes, and a very mild cheese flavor. However, there's one major difference between cottage cheese and mayonnaise: Texture. Straight out of the plastic tub, cottage cheese can be, well, lumpy. This may not bother you in the slightest, but if it does, there's an easy workaround: Whipping the cottage cheese. You can do this with a hand mixer, mini food processor, or even just a big fork; the goal being to break those curds into a finer texture similar to ricotta. You can use the same technique to incorporate this high-protein food into smoothies, dips, and even macaroni and cheese.

Hummus was the "it" food product of the early 2000s, but in the years since, it has faded in popularity. Maybe we were just given too much, too fast: Beet hummus, carrot hummus, lentil hummus, chocolate hummus — each variation obfuscating the beauty of this simple, timeless, life-sustaining food. Hummus, the type made from chickpeas, sesame paste (tahini), and olive oil, is an ancient form of plant-based protein foundational to Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines. When blended, the ingredients make a velvety emulsion that — depending on how much ice water or oil you use — can be spread or scooped over everything, from bulgur wheat to falafel wraps.

It's also a great addition to salads — including ones made from chicken. Here, hummus provides an extra protein boost as well as some much-needed fattiness. Its blend of Middle Eastern spices — cumin, sumac, garlic, za'atar — contributes a warmth and brightness that cuts through the inherent blandness of cooked chicken breast. If using hummus as the foundation of your chicken salad, consider adding other Mediterranean ingredients, like capers, olives, walnuts, almonds, fresh tomato, or cucumbers. You can use your favorite supermarket brand, or just quickly whip up delicious hummus at home.

Probably the most underrated ingredient on this list, silken tofu is a centuries-old, plant-based protein with limitless applications. Like other forms of bean curd, silken tofu is made from soybeans, but it's worlds different from soft, medium, or firm varieties. While it comes in similar packaging, silken tofu is hardly solid; it's more like a pudding or flan that will fall apart if you try to pick it up with a fork. However, it's precisely this loose creaminess that makes silken tofu such a terrific substitute for mayonnaise in your next chicken salad.

Besides being a great protein source — containing around 20 grams per 16-ounce package — silken tofu can easily be made smooth and pourable. When blended, it becomes something akin to Alfredo sauce, with a velvety consistency that's ideal for coating chicken. Another advantage of silken tofu is its taste — or lack thereof. You're dealing with a blank canvas here, one that will quickly absorb whatever seasonings, herbs, or sauces you mix with it. It may need some doctoring to get the texture right, but just use this as another opportunity to add flavor. Try adding cilantro and lime, tarragon and sherry vinegar, or hot sauce, for a Buffalo wing-inspired chicken salad.

There are only so many ways to add creaminess to food without relying on dairy, a fatty emulsion, or some complicated form of food chemistry. Adding a can of blended beans is one of them. Legumes, like black beans, kidney beans, and butter beans, have a starchy center that turns smooth and pillowy when blended. Most commercial varieties you find at your typical supermarket are good for cooking, but some have a more distinct flavor than others.

When making chicken salad, it's best to use beans with a clean, neat taste and not too much earthiness. For this, white, cannellini, or Great Northern beans are best. They won't overwhelm the other ingredients in your chicken salad, but they also aren't entirely neutral-tasting, either. The key to using these legumes is to purée them with different spices, herbs, and condiments, like Worcestershire sauce, miso, or a splash of vinegar. To achieve a texture that's similar to mayonnaise, you'll likely need to add some liquid or fat. Olive or another neutral oil works, but adding a heavily seasoned broth will give you an even better result. To do this, make a quick pan sauce with sautéed aromatics, seasonings, and stock; add it to your beans, then blend everything in a blender or food processor.

This one is a little sneaky. Egg yolks are inherently fatty, but they also contain natural emulsifiers that turn into a creamy paste when blended. That means you don't have to add a drop of mayonnaise (which, ironically, is made predominantly from egg yolks) to achieve a luscious texture. But egg salad brings more to the party than just creaminess. If you've ever watched a TikTok nutritionist worth their creatine, then you're probably frustratingly aware that egg whites are one of nature's purest protein sources.

This combination of smooth, fatty yolk and protein-rich white makes egg salad an incredible substitute for mayo. It's a tongue-in-cheek pairing, for sure, but this whimsical culinary mashup also delivers on taste. Because eggs are a tad sulfurous on their own, season them generously with ingredients like Dijon mustard, capers, lemon juice, smoked paprika, or even a few shakes of curry powder. However, the key to achieving a natural creaminess is proper egg cookery, which essentially boils down to not overcooking your hard-boiled eggs. The answer: A quick dunk in the ice bath for about 10-15 minutes to halt cooking and preserve those fluffy yolks.

Want the nutritional upside of yogurt with an added burst of refreshing Mediterranean flavors? Sounds like it's tzatziki time. The yogurt-based dip is most closely associated with Greek cuisine, serving as a cooling counterpoint to robustly seasoned grilled meats, fried zucchini, and platters of pita. And, while its protein content isn't on the same level as skyr or cottage cheese, it isn't negligible, either, which is why it's another smart mayo substitute for your next chicken salad.

Tzatziki looks simple, but it delivers a chorus of complex flavors that few condiments can match. It's all things smooth, rich, tangy, and fresh, thanks to a blend of fresh herbs and other aromatics. Besides yogurt, the predominant ingredient is cucumber. Paired with fresh mint, dill, and garlic, this creates a clean, powerful taste profile. It instantly elevates ordinary chicken into something moist and tender. Slip your tzatziki-coated chicken salad into a pita and top with shredded lettuce, tomato, black olives, and sliced red onion for a memorable lunch. While tzatziki is popular, it can be difficult to find good options in your average supermarket. Thankfully, a quality tzatziki sauce is easy to put together; just remember to squeeze the moisture out of your cucumbers. Otherwise, your sauce will be too wet and separate.

Labneh is made by straining Greek yogurt in cheesecloth until you remove the remaining liquid whey. This not only creates a denser product, but it also concentrates the flavor. It's traditionally made with goat's milk, which is a little grassy on the palate and has a slightly tangier finish than a cow's milk cheese or yogurt. Unlike yogurt, though, which you typically eat with a spoon, labneh is more of a dip, perfect for crudités, pita, lavash, or even grilled fruits. It has a decadent mouthfeel and is decidedly more savory, especially when dressed with olive oil, making it a nice way to rejuvenate an otherwise tired chicken salad.

But there's no reason to pigeonhole this spreadable yogurt as savory or sweet; it works beautifully with both taste profiles. You can roll it in za'atar, sumac, and fresh mint, or crust it with pistachios and drizzle it with honey. Since it's the thickest yogurt-based product on this list, when using it for chicken salad, you'll likely want to add a splash of milk or a non-dairy alternative to loosen it up. If you can't find labneh in stores, you can literally just add Greek yogurt to a cheesecloth, hang it above your sink, and let it drip for a few hours until it's firm and extra creamy.

Like most dairy products, feta is a solid protein source, with about 4 grams per 2-ounce serving; however, it differs from other cheeses because it's brined in a salt-water and whey solution rather than traditionally aged. This process helps preserve the cheese while also imbuing it with its signature salinity. If you've been lucky enough to try quality feta, you know that this soft, crumbly cheese packs a punch. In the mouth, it has a clean, fresh cream flavor and mild tang, making it a natural partner for grilled meats like beef, lamb, or chicken.

Feta isn't spreadable, nor does it melt, but you can easily transform its texture by dropping a few chunks into a blender or food processor and "whipping" it until smooth. The result is smooth, salty, and spoonable — and perfect for chicken salad. When using whipped feta, consider both its salt content and mild acidic bite. These are strong flavors that should be balanced with other sweet and savory ingredients. Try pairing it with starchy, nutty, or mildly sweet foods like roasted butternut squash, pistachios, dried cranberries, or nectarines.

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.
